analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to override state water pollution decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 13, 2013 with just two cosponsors, one from each party, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Water Act so that once a state approves a water quality standard or a pollution permit, the EPA could not override it, object to it, or impose a stricter federal version unless the state agrees. It would also block the EPA's power to veto permits that fill in wetlands and streams unless the state where the discharge originates concurs, cut the time federal agencies get to comment on permit applications from 90 days to 30, and require the EPA to publish state-by-state job and economic impact analyses before issuing new water rules. All of this would apply immediately, including to permit applications already pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that need federal water permits would gain the most: mining companies that bury streams with mine waste, developers that fill wetlands, and industrial or municipal dischargers. For them, a state permit would become effectively final — the EPA could not object to it, withdraw a state's permitting authority, or veto a wetland-filling permit, even where it disagrees with how the state applies water quality standards. States that want faster permitting would also gain authority.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from issuing a new or stricter water quality standard for any pollutant already covered by a state standard the EPA has approved, unless the state itself concurs.

Bars the EPA from superseding a state's finding that a discharge complies with the Clean Water Act, and from objecting to individual state-issued permits or withdrawing a state's permitting program over disagreements about how standards or federal guidance are implemented.
Blocks the EPA's veto of dredge-and-fill permits — the tool used to stop projects that bury streams and wetlands — unless the state where the discharge originates agrees the harm is unacceptable.
Cuts the window for federal agencies to comment on permit applications from 90 days to 30 (or 60 on request), speeding approvals.

Requires the EPA, before any new water rule or guidance, to analyze job and economic effects state by state, hold hearings and post notices in states losing more than 100 jobs or $1 million in economic activity.

analysis.who_pays: People downstream would bear the cost. The bill lets only the state where a discharge originates decide whether to allow it, so a neighboring state receiving the polluted water would have no federal recourse. Drinking-water supplies, fisheries, and wetlands would depend solely on each state's own enforcement, with no federal backstop when a state's decisions fall short.

drawbacks.text: Once a state approves a permit or standard, no federal check remains — not even where the EPA disagrees with the state's implementation of its own approved standards or of federal guidance interpreting them.

Only the state where a discharge originates gets to concur in the EPA's finding of unacceptable harm, so discharges flowing into downstream or neighboring states could proceed over the objections of the people they affect.
The changes apply retroactively to permit applications already pending and standards already being written, changing the rules in the middle of ongoing reviews.

The required jobs analysis is one-directional by design: the bill forbids counting any offsetting job or economic gains in the loss calculation, so the published analysis would systematically overstate harm from EPA actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case is real: state agencies handle the day-to-day permitting, federal second-guessing of approved state decisions can duplicate work and slow projects, and permit delays cost jobs — the jobs-analysis and hearing provisions address a genuine complaint. But the remedy is disproportionate. Rather than speeding federal review, the bill makes state decisions effectively unreviewable — including for downstream states and permits already in the pipeline — and removes the Clean Water Act's core design feature: a federal backstop when state protection fails. A narrower bill setting firm deadlines without eliminating federal overrides would have captured most of the promised benefit at far less cost to water quality.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2013, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its water subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative John Mica introduced the bill on May 13, 2013, joined by original cosponsors Representatives Nick Rahall, a Democrat, and Bob Gibbs, a Republican.
The House referred it the same day to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to that committee's Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill sat at the subcommittee for the remaining twenty months of the 113th Congress and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

The bill would have barred the EPA from overriding state water quality standards, superseding state discharge determinations, objecting to state-issued permits, or vetoing dredge-and-fill permits without state concurrence, with all changes applying to pending applications.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary water users won by default: because the bill died, the EPA kept the authority it would have lost to second-guess state water decisions. The mining, development, and discharger interests the bill was written for gained nothing new, but also lost nothing — the permitting status quo simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream communities; EPA kept its oversight

for.name: Rep. John Mica
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on May 13, 2013.

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor — the bill's only Democratic supporter.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; after its referral to the water subcommittee on May 14, 2013, the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Issued a formal 2011 statement against the identical bill in the prior Congress, saying the President's senior advisers would recommend a veto; no statement was needed for this reintroduction because it never advanced that far.

sides.party_line_note: The only test of support was sponsorship: a Republican sponsor joined by one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor (two in all), and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll calls show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The EPA's veto power over dredge-and-fill permits and its tighter readings of state standards have fallen hardest on mining projects that bury streams with mine waste; this bill would take away both tools unless the mining state itself agreed. Cheaper, faster, final permits for the industry come at the cost of stream and water quality for communities below the mine.
With the EPA unable to veto permits that fill wetlands without state concurrence, approvals would speed up and wetland loss would land on nearby residents as added flood risk and lost open space.

industries.industry: Industrial and municipal dischargers holding pollution permits
industries.note: State-issued discharge permits would become effectively final; the EPA could not object even where it reads the applicable water quality standards or federal guidance differently, lowering the risk of retrofit costs.

The bill locks in state agencies as the final word on water quality within their own borders, which supporters call cooperative federalism and states genuinely value. The same finality removes protection for downstream states and leaves permit decisions with no federal backstop when a state falls short.
